headline: Thailand revokes 24 cannabis shop licences, suspends 105 in FY2026
dek: Thailand's traditional medicine department said on 21 November it revoked 24 cannabis shop licences and suspended 105 in fiscal 2026, and will target school areas.
key_points: Thailand's Department of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine said on 21 November that it revoked 24 cannabis business licences and suspended 105 in fiscal 2026, the year that ended in September.
Its 95 enforcement operations led to 70 arrests and the seizure of 10,584.9 kg of cannabis and related material, with damage it valued at 223.5 million baht.
Bangkok has 1,710 licensed cannabis premises, the most of any province; inspectors have checked 1,437 of them, about 84%, and say they will speed up the remaining 273.
For fiscal 2027 the department plans wider routine inspections, a focus on shops near schools and faster action on public complaints.
body: Thailand has given the clearest figures yet on how hard it is policing the cannabis shops that spread across the country after it loosened its cannabis rules. Officials at the Department of Thai Traditional and Alternative Medicine (DTAM), part of the Ministry of Public Health, said on Saturday 21 November that during fiscal 2026 they revoked 24 cannabis business licences and suspended 105 others, The Nation reported.

The figures cover the whole fiscal year, which ran to the end of September, not a single new sweep. They were presented by Dr Thewan Thaneerat, the department's deputy director-general, and Dr Peeracha Kukasemkit, who directs its Division of Medical Cannabis, according to The Nation and The Thaiger. Thai outlets spell both names in several ways.

The department said its officers carried out 95 enforcement operations in the year. Those led to 70 arrests and the seizure or impoundment of 10,584.9 kg of cannabis and related materials. It put the economic damage connected to the cases at 223.5 million baht, which Bangkok-based outlet The Globe converts to about US$6.9 million.

On MetaFlora's arithmetic, that is 129 licences revoked or suspended in all, and an average of about 111 kg of material seized per operation. The damage estimate works out at roughly 2.35 million baht per operation. The department did not publish a breakdown of which licence conditions were broken, and none of the reports we read lists the specific violations behind the revocations.
> Thailand is no longer asking whether to police its cannabis shops, only how many inspectors it can put through the door.

Bangkok has 1,710 licensed cannabis premises, more than any other province, the department said. Its inspectors have visited 1,437 of them, or 84.04%. The other 273, about 16% of the capital's licensed premises, have not yet been inspected, and officials said they would speed that work up. The figure describes how far the inspection programme has got, not how many shops are breaking the rules.

Officials also gave one example of how complaints reach them. On 16 September the Division of Medical Cannabis checked six premises in Bangkok's Watthana district after residents filed complaints through Traffy Fondue, the city's public reporting platform. The findings were passed to the licensing authority to decide what action to take, The Thaiger reported.

The department's plan for fiscal 2027, which began in October, has four parts, according to The Globe and The Nation. It will expand routine inspections of licensed businesses across the country. It will check compliance with the conditions attached to licences to sell and process cannabis. It will pay particular attention to shops near schools and other educational institutions. And it will respond faster to complaints from the public.

The school focus is the clearest signal of political priorities. Shops clustered in tourist and residential districts have been the most visible face of Thailand's cannabis trade, and the department's framing of its work, as enforcement of the legal framework for medical use, shows how far official language has moved from the open market of the first years after the rules were loosened.

For investors and suppliers, Thailand has been a test of what happens when a country opens cannabis retail quickly and regulates afterwards. The fiscal 2026 numbers suggest that the correction is being done shop by shop, through licence conditions and inspections, not through a single new law. A licence that can be suspended or revoked on inspection is worth less to a buyer or lender than one with settled rules, which matters for anyone valuing Thai retail assets or selling into the market.

The scale is also worth keeping in proportion. On the department's figures, 129 enforcement actions on licences in a year is a small share of Bangkok's 1,710 licensed premises alone, before counting the rest of the country. The department did not give a national total of licensed businesses in the reports we read, so the share of all Thai licences affected cannot be calculated from these figures.

Watch whether the department publishes the violation categories behind the 129 actions, which would show whether it is chasing unlicensed sales, location rules or record keeping. Watch the pace of the remaining 273 Bangkok inspections. And watch whether the school-zone focus turns into a formal distance rule, which would force relocations rather than case-by-case action.
